## Overview

Karelians are a Baltic Finnic ethnic group indigenous to the historical region of Karelia, now divided between Finland and Russia. In Finland, “Karelian” generally refers to Finnish Karelians, including Karelian-speaking communities formerly living in the easternmost parts of Finnish Karelia, known as *Raja-Karjala* or “Border Karelia.” Russian Karelians mainly live in the Republic of Karelia and adjacent north-western areas, with enclaves in the Tver and Novgorod oblasts. The Karelian language is closely related to Finnish. Karelians traditionally speak Karelian and are associated with Eastern Orthodox Christianity, although western Karelians were also shaped by Roman Catholic and Lutheran history. Their importance in folk culture is especially documented through Karelian folklore, tales, and epic poetry collected into the *Kalevala*.

## Festivals & rituals

They do document religious and historical changes affecting Karelian communities. Karelians traditionally included Eastern Orthodox Christians, while western Karelians became first Roman Catholic and later Lutheran. Folk beliefs were widely incorporated into Christianity among Orthodox Karelians. In 1314, Karelians rose against efforts to convert them to Christianity, and the rebellion spread through Karelian lands. In the 19th century, Karelianism shaped Finnish artistic and research interest in Orthodox Karelians, who were regarded as having preserved elements of an archaic Finnish culture.

## Oral tradition & literature

Karelian tales, along with some Finnish tales, were collected to form the *Kalevala*. During the 19th century, Finnish folklorists, including Elias Lönnrot, travelled to different parts of Eastern Karelia to gather folklore and epic poetry. This collection activity formed part of the broader process of “finnisation” in Finland and contributed to Karelianism, an ideology that inspired Finnish artists and researchers.

## Language & religion

Karelian is a Baltic Finnic language closely related to Finnish. The sources identify North Karelian, South Karelian, Tver Karelian, and Olonets Karelian or Livvi. North Karelian is spoken in the northern parts of the Republic of Karelia and in some villages near the Russian border in the Kainuu region. South Karelian is associated with the southern parts of the Republic of Karelia and with locations in Finland and elsewhere after World War II. Tver Karelian is spoken in the Tver area of Russia, while Olonets Karelian or Livvi is spoken in south-eastern parts of the Republic of Karelia. Ludic, spoken in the easternmost part of the Republic of Karelia, is currently considered a language of its own. Most Russian Karelians are Eastern Orthodox Christians, and folk beliefs have been widely incorporated into Orthodox Christianity. Lutheran revivalistic movements, including Laestadianism, were influential among Karelian towns in the 20th century.
